hook.text: Eighty percent of the world's population relies on traditional medicine. It's not alternative — it's the mainstream.

buildup.text: Traditional medicine includes herbal remedies, spiritual healing, and bodywork passed down through generations.

discovery.text: These systems often treat the whole person — body, mind, spirit, and social relations — not just isolated symptoms.

twist.text: Many modern drugs owe debts to traditional knowledge. Aspirin from willow bark, quinine from cinchona bark.

climax.text: Traditional medicine isn't outdated. It's a living system of knowledge that biomedicine is only beginning to respect.

punchline.text: The oldest medicine is still the most widely used.

quiz.question: How much of the world uses traditional medicine?

details.summary: Traditional medicine encompasses healing systems developed within specific cultures over centuries, including herbal remedies, spiritual healing, and body-based therapies. These systems often integrate physical, spiritual, and social dimensions of health that biomedicine separates.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional medicine serves the primary healthcare needs of billions of people. Dismissing it as superstition ignores both its empirical effectiveness for certain conditions and its cultural importance to communities.
takeaways: Traditional medicine includes herbal, spiritual, and body-based healing
It serves primary healthcare for billions worldwide
These systems integrate physical, spiritual, and social health dimensions

faq.question: Does traditional medicine actually work?
faq.answer: Some traditional remedies have proven bioactive compounds — aspirin derives from willow bark, artemisinin from traditional Chinese medicine. Other practices work through placebo, social support, or stress reduction.

faq.question: What are the risks of traditional medicine?
faq.answer: Herbal remedies can interact dangerously with pharmaceuticals. Some practices delay effective biomedical treatment. Unregulated preparation can produce contaminated or inconsistent doses. Medical anthropologists advocate informed integration rather than blanket acceptance or rejection.
